title: NIO owner falls asleep at 110 km/h on a rainy highway, and his car's emergency pull-over function stops it while an SOS call wakes him
summary: The emergency pull-over function of the NIO World Model, NIO's assisted-driving software, stopped a car whose driver fell asleep at 110 km/h on 1 June 2025, and an SOS call woke him.
account: On 30 May 2025 NIO began pushing the first release of its NIO World Model to more than 400,000 Banyan-platform cars. The release added an emergency autonomous pull-over function. CnEVPost reports that before this release NIO cars could only slow and stop in their own lane when a driver stopped responding. Around midnight on 1 June 2025, a NIO owner fell asleep driving at 110 km/h on a highway in rain in China. NIO's assisted driving was engaged. The emergency autonomous pull-over function triggered, and an SOS call woke him. He posted a video on social media on 2 June. NIO founder William Li reposted it and described the function: gradual deceleration, a lane change to the rightmost emergency lane, hazard lights and an SOS intervention. He stressed that assisted driving is not autonomous driving. No crash or injury was reported. The sources do not name the vehicle model or the highway. On 28 January 2026 NIO rolled out a major update of the software to more than 460,000 Banyan-system vehicles. In October 2026 Kuai Keji relayed another NIO owner's account. She said that she was taken ill on an elevated road with her daughter, and that assisted driving and the NOMI assistant got the car to the roadside and called for help.
purpose: NIO's first NWM release, pushed to Banyan-platform cars from 30 May 2025, added an “emergency autonomous pull-over”. It works on a highway or urban expressway when the assisted-driving system detects an unresponsive driver. The car slows gradually, moves to the rightmost emergency lane, turns on its hazard lights and triggers an SOS call. CnEVPost notes that NIO cars previously could only decelerate and stop within the current lane. This event is that function doing what it was built to do.
system: NIO World Model (NWM) emergency autonomous pull-over function within NIO's assisted-driving system
model_version: First release of NIO World Model (NWM), pushed to more than 400,000 Banyan-platform cars from 30 May 2025; the vehicle model and software build are not reported
segment: Consumer driver-assistance software on a privately owned vehicle

ratings.reason: One identifiable driver, asleep at 110 km/h in rain on a highway, was brought to a stop and woken without a crash. The owner's account, as relayed by the outlets, calls it a rescue (“挽救”). The account does not establish that a crash was imminent.

ai_role.statement: The NWM-based assisted-driving system judged the driver unresponsive, ran the emergency pull-over and placed the SOS call that woke him. The car was already under assisted driving. Its specific contribution was therefore taking the car out of the live lane and rousing the driver rather than keeping it in lane. The sequence is known only from the owner's video as relayed by independent outlets. NIO's founder confirmed the function's design. No telemetry, police report or third-party verification was published.

fields.summary: The emergency pull-over function of the NIO World Model, NIO's assisted-driving software, stopped a car whose driver fell asleep at 110 km/h on 1 June 2025, and an SOS call woke him.
fields.account: On 30 May 2025 NIO began pushing the first release of its NIO World Model to more than 400,000 Banyan-platform cars. The release added an emergency autonomous pull-over function. CnEVPost reports that before this release NIO cars could only slow and stop in their own lane when a driver stopped responding. Around midnight on 1 June 2025, a NIO owner fell asleep driving at 110 km/h on a highway in rain in China. NIO's assisted driving was engaged. The emergency autonomous pull-over function triggered, and an SOS call woke him. He posted a video on social media on 2 June. NIO founder William Li reposted it and described the function: gradual deceleration, a lane change to the rightmost emergency lane, hazard lights and an SOS intervention. He stressed that assisted driving is not autonomous driving. No crash or injury was reported. The sources do not name the vehicle model or the highway. On 28 January 2026 NIO rolled out a major update of the software to more than 460,000 Banyan-system vehicles. In October 2026 Kuai Keji relayed another NIO owner's account. She said that she was taken ill on an elevated road with her daughter, and that assisted driving and the NOMI assistant got the car to the roadside and called for help.
